title: Born in two halves
hookLine: Yudhishthira wants to give up; Bhima argues for effort, and Krishna tells how Jarasandha was born in two halves
carry: daiva and effort: you still do your part

cards: Yudhishthira hears about Jarasandha and does something unexpected. He backs down. If even Krishna's people fled from this man, he says, how can we stand against him?
Let's give up the sacrifice. Peace is better. It's a startling thing to hear from the man whose father asked for this.
Then his brothers speak, one after the other. And Krishna tells a story about how Jarasandha came to be born.

teach.b: Bhima speaks first, and bluntly. A king who never makes an effort, he says, wears down like an anthill. Then a plan: Krishna's wisdom, my strength, Arjuna's skill.
Krishna and Arjuna argue for it too. Yudhishthira's caution isn't mocked. It's answered.
Hindu thought has names for the two sides of this argument: daiva, what's given, fate, the hand of the gods; and purushakara, human effort.
The Mahabharata keeps setting them side by side, and the reading most teachers give is that you need both. You can't control how it turns out, but that never excuses not doing your part.
Then Krishna tells where the enemy came from. A king of Magadha named Brihadratha had two wives and no son.

A sage, Chandakaushika, gave him a single fruit to bring a son. The king divided it between his two wives, so neither would be left out. Each queen gave birth to half a child: one eye, one arm, one leg each.
Horrified, the queens had the halves left outside.

A rakshasi named Jara found them, and as she picked them up, the halves joined into one strong child. She carried him back to the king, and in the epic's telling, Magadha held a festival in her honor.
The text says his name comes from her: Jarasandha, the one joined by Jara.
Even here, the two meet: a sage's gift, a father's fair choice, a stranger's hands. The strength was given to him. What he did with it was his.
Tomorrow, the three set out for Magadha, and not dressed as warriors.

how: The story of Jarasandha's birth is told in the Sabha Parva of the Mahabharata, which Hindus read, hear recited and see performed as part of the epic.

o: a war council held before marching on Magadha
a sage's gift of one fruit to bring a king a son
the royal rite Yudhishthira almost gave up for peace

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: a king who makes no effort wears down

s: Yudhishthira was eager to fight Jarasandha
he wanted to give up the sacrifice and keep the peace.
Jarasandha was born as two halves
each queen bore half a child, and Jara joined them.
Hindu teaching says if it's fated, effort doesn't matter
the epic sets daiva beside purushakara; most teachers say you need both.

games.q: you're Yudhishthira. the enemy is strong, and you're tempted to say 'if it's meant to be, it'll happen.' Bhima says that's how kings wear down. what's the answer?
o: do your part, and leave the outcome to God.
games.why: daiva and purushakara together: the outcome isn't yours to control, but the effort is. Yudhishthira takes up the plan.

practice: Pick one thing you've been tempted to give up on because it looks too big. Many Hindus begin any effort by bowing to Ganesha, remover of obstacles, and then doing the work.
If you pray, say softly, om gam ganapataye namah, and offer the outcome to God. If you don't, simply name the next small step. Either way, the result isn't yours to control.

wordCard.voice: The Rajasuya. Today, the sacrifice nearly given up, then taken back up, with effort, a plan and a story about the enemy's birth.

orig.note: Sanskrit jarāsandha: the text explains the name as 'joined by Jara', the rakshasi who joined his two halves.

carryVoice: Your line: daiva and effort, you still do your part. Bhima wouldn't let his king wear down like an anthill. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Rajasuyarambha and Jarasandha-vadha Parvas (Yudhishthira's hesitation; Bhima's and Arjuna's speeches; the birth of Jarasandha)
Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva (Bhishma answers Yudhishthira on destiny and human exertion)
